newsitem.title: NICARAGUA: For richer or poorer, Nicaragua votes.
newsitem.headline: For richer or poorer, Nicaragua votes.

text.p: From the mansions on Managua's breezy hills to the bleak hovels in its misery belt, Nicaraguans voted on Sunday in a presidential election as polarised as the lives of its long-suffering people.

Tapping her foot impatiently as she waited in line to vote in Managua's exclusive Santo Domingo neighbourhood, housewife Maria Alicia Cesar, Indian maid in tow, railed against left- wing presidential candidate Daniel Ortega, whose last-minute surge in the polls has terrified Nicaragua's tiny elite.
"I have to wait here as long as it takes. That horrible man (Ortega) can't win the election after all he has done," Cesar, 26, said, after driving up to vote in a plush Toyota Land Cruiser.

"Some of my friends have said they'll leave the country if he wins," she added, casting a vote for the burly former mayor of Managua, right-wing Arnoldo Aleman, who narrowly led Ortega ahead of the vote.
Many wealthy Nicaraguans remember Ortega as the fiery Marxist leader who ruled Nicaragua from 1979 to 1990, confiscating property from the rich and introducing a planned economy.
Some of the better off fled to comfortable lives in Miami, and planes from the United States last week were packed with die-hard exiles singing anthems of support for Aleman as they flew to Managua.

In the mean streets of Managua's poor San Jose Barrio, Consuela Palacios, 18, waited for hours on a rutted, dirt road in front of a makeshift shack with a plastic door that served as a voting station.
"Daniel's the only one who cares about the poor," said Consuela Palacios, a Sandinista red-and-black heart painted under her left eye.
Palacios' neighbours, knowing that in Nicaragua nothing happens quickly, brought plastic chairs and soda pop, and reacted with resignation when their voting station opened two hours late.

"We're in Nicaragua, we know what to expect," said unemployed mechanic Mario Gutierrez, 42, moving his chair slowly forward every five minutes as the line advanced. "I'll vote for Ortega because at least I had work when he was in power," a shirtless Gutierrez said.

Many of Nicaragua's poor fondly remember the early years of Ortega's Sandinista government when everyone had beans, tortillas and free medical care. Some forget the later years when the economy fell apart, and a bloody war between the Sandinistas and U.S.-backed Contra rebels left 25,000 dead.
Many mistrust Ortega's snappy conversion from renegade Marxist who drafted hundreds of thousands of young Nicaraguans into the Contra war into a self-styled moderate, pro-business social democrat.
"If Ortega wins this country is ruined," said Josefa Gomez, a 71-year-old matriarch in a poor neighbourhood, shading herself with a pink umbrella.
Among the poor, Aleman stirs mixed emotions. Some fear his alleged links to ex-dictator Anastasio Somoza, while others say he has the clout to get things done and stand up to the Sandinistas.
With 54 percent of Nicaraguans unemployed and its street lights crowded with hungry, begging children, the poor now form the bulk of the electorate and will decide who wins Sunday's vote.
